title: Tier-resolution shim so the 4 single-agent plugins stop hardcoding model in frontmatter
idea: mission-control, unifi, deploy, and home-lab-ops each ship exactly one agent whose `model:` is a frozen frontmatter literal (verified: 1 each), with no way to run them at a cheaper or heavier tier for a given invocation. Add a lightweight `tier:` frontmatter convention (`tier: judgment|mechanical|survey`) plus a resolver that maps the semantic tier to a concrete `{model, effort}` from the canonical palette at spawn/skill-load, so a home-lab preflight can drop to survey-tier and a deploy gate can escalate to judgment-tier without editing frontmatter. The mapping table is one file; the operator overrides per run. This propagates the effort dimension (absent everywhere outside saga) into the single-agent plugins for the first time.

title: A per-unit tier floor so upgrade-only segment merge can't cheap out a must-be-deep unit
idea: `segment_units()` derives a segment's tier by upgrade-only index arithmetic — `min(MODELS.index)` / `max(EFFORTS.index)` (`execution_spec.py:1474-1475`) — which means a cheap unit sharing a segment can only ever be pulled UP, but there is no way to assert 'this adversarial-review unit must never resolve below opus/high' as an invariant the merge respects. Add an optional `min_tier` on `Unit` that `segment_units()` clamps the merged tier up to, and fail emit if a declared floor is itself off-palette. This gives the ordered ladder a floor concept to complement its ceiling, so a security or design unit carries a guaranteed minimum through segment collapse instead of hoping the merge math lands high enough.

Crosses `{#tier-vocab-ordering}` — engaged by implementing the floor as index arithmetic over the SAME ordered tuples (clamp = max over MODELS-strength index), preserving the load-bearing ordering contract the learning at LEARNINGS.md:164 protects rather than adding an unordered override.
outcome_shape: PR adding `Unit.min_tier` + clamp in `segment_units()` + validate + round-trip in `to_dict`, with `tests/test_saga_execution_spec.py` cases: floor pulls a cheap segment up, off-palette floor fails emit, absent floor round-trips byte-identical. Verified: new tests green, existing spec golden tests unchanged.

title: Auto-escalate one rung up the ladder on unit HALT instead of manual re-tiering
idea: Tier tuples are ordered escalation ladders (#tier-vocab-ordering), and segment_units already steps them via min(MODELS.index)/max(EFFORTS.index) index arithmetic — but when a unit HALTs or its output fails the gate, escalation is a manual operator act: notice, re-tier, re-run. Automate it: an opt-in escalation policy on a unit that, on gate failure, retries once at the next rung up the ladder (stronger model or higher effort via the existing index math) before surfacing the HALT to the operator. The best version of 'operator manually bumps the tier and reruns' is no step — the ladder that already exists in code drives the retry.

The ordered ladder is already load-bearing machinery; auto-escalation reuses it rather than adding new ordering semantics, so it builds on the binding decision rather than contradicting it.

Introduce a fleet rule that every agent must declare an effort (or a role-tier that resolves one), enforced by a marketplace-CI guard the same way plugin.json fields are checked. title: Promote the ladder from tuple-index-arithmetic to an explicit named-rung data structure
idea: {#tier-vocab-ordering} establishes that MODELS/EFFORTS are ordered ladders, but the ordering is encoded only as position in a tuple plus a load-bearing comment, and 'is A stronger than B' / 'escalate one rung' are re-implemented as scattered min(MODELS.index)/max(EFFORTS.index) arithmetic. That near-miss (appending fable would have silently ranked it weaker than haiku) is the tell that index-in-a-tuple is the wrong representation. Reframe the palette as a first-class ladder: an ordered list of rungs each with an explicit rank and a strength comparator, exposing rank(model), stronger_of(a,b), and escalate(tier, rungs=1) as functions. segment_units and any future consumer call the ladder API instead of doing index math, so adding a model can never silently invert strength.

Binding register affirms tiers are ordered escalation ladders; this idea structurally encodes that decision rather than contradicting it.
outcome_shape: PR refactoring plugins/saga/scripts/execution_spec.py to derive an explicit ladder object (rank + comparator API) from the palette, replacing the min/max .index() call sites in segment_units, plus a test asserting a new model inserted at any rung yields the intended strength order. Verified by existing test_segment_tier_merge_prefers_fable_and_xhigh plus a new insert-a-model regression staying green.

title: Climb the ladder at runtime — auto-escalate one rung on budget-exhaustion or refutation instead of halting
idea: The ordered ladder exists but is only ever read at authoring time; at runtime the machinery only halts. When a cheap-tier agent exhausts its StructuredOutput budget or a verify panel refutes a unit, the run stops rather than doing the one thing an escalation LADDER is for: retry the same unit one rung stronger. Reframe the ladder as a dynamic climb, not a static label. Add an opt-in escalation policy: on a bounded set of failure signatures (budget-exhaustion, verifier-disagreement), re-dispatch the failed unit at the next rung up (haiku→sonnet→opus, effort medium→high→xhigh) once, then halt if still failing. This spends premium tokens only where cheap tiers demonstrably failed — the inverse of xhigh-Opus-on-everything.
basis: First-principles: execution_spec.py bakes BUDGET_RIDER precisely because cheap-tier agents exhaust budget (lines 122-129), and the emitter throws verifier-disagreement / missing-output on refutation or short output — both are terminal halts today. An ordering that is defined (MODELS/EFFORTS, {#tier-vocab-ordering}) but never traversed at runtime is latent capability: the same index-arithmetic that computes a merged tier can compute 'the next rung,' so escalate-and-retry is a small addition atop existing structure, and it directly answers the session-mining pain 'xhigh-Opus on everything is wasteful' by escalating reactively rather than pre-emptively. Extends, does not contradict, {#tier-vocab-ordering}.
outcome_shape: PR adding an opt-in escalate-on-failure policy (config flag + next-rung helper) to the emitted workflow harness / team-execution retry path, bounded to one climb, emitting a visible escalation log line. Verified by a test where a unit fails at haiku, is re-dispatched at sonnet, and the run continues; and a second test asserting the climb halts after one rung.

Adding a model becomes a one-line manifest edit; the drift guard catches any file that hardcodes a stale or off-palette model.

title: Invert ownership: teammates declare a tier FLOOR; the plan may escalate above it but never under-tier it
idea: The QUEUED seed assumes the plan (or operator) is the sole authority that assigns each teammate its effort. But the real failure mode is the opposite: reviewers carry no model field and silently inherit whatever the session default is, so a cheap session can run the security or architecture reviewer at haiku without anyone deciding to. Reframe WHO owns the tier: let each teammate declare its own minimum-viable tier FLOOR in its frontmatter (security-reviewer floor = opus/high), and let the plan's per-teammate table only escalate above that floor, never below. This flips the seed from 'plan dictates effort down' to 'agent guarantees a floor, plan tunes up' — so under-tiering a judgment reviewer becomes structurally impossible rather than a silent session accident.

Verified by that clamp test plus a live team-execute run showing the reviewer spawned at its floor despite a cheaper session default.

title: Tier vocabulary as an authoritative DNS zone with generated resolvers
idea: Extract MODELS/EFFORTS (and the ordered ladder metadata) out of execution_spec.py into one authoritative tier_vocabulary.py module that both execution_spec.py and outcome_spec.py import, instead of hand-maintaining parallel copies guarded by a drift test. Model it on DNS: one authoritative zone-of-record, and every other consumer is a read-only resolver that imports rather than redeclares. Ship a tiny `tier_resolver.py resolve <alias>` CLI so any plugin's agent-loader or team-execution emitter can query the canonical set at load time rather than embedding a literal. The current drift-guard test that asserts two copies stay byte-identical becomes an import assertion — the mirror stops being a copy and becomes a pointer, which is the DNS 'single record, many caches' invariant.

Seam it attaches to: execution_spec.py:52-53 defines MODELS/EFFORTS as module-local tuples, and the module docstring at :80-81 documents that outcome_spec.py mirrors SANDBOX_PROFILES verbatim behind a cross-module drift-guard test — i.e. the fleet already pays the hand-copy-plus-guard tax the DNS pattern eliminates.

title: Effort as a DSCP class marking carried in agent frontmatter
idea: Add an `effort:` field to agent frontmatter across the fleet as a first-class dimension alongside `model:`, borrowing the DiffServ/DSCP model from packet networks: every packet carries a small class marking (a first-class header field) that routers honor per-hop rather than re-deriving it. Today every one of the 24 team-execution agents (and all frontmatter fleet-wide) hardcodes `model:` and carries zero `effort:`, so effort is invisible until saga's plan tier-table re-invents it per run. Give each agent a declared effort marking that the dispatch/agent-loader honors, defaulting to the model's historical effort when absent (Postel-style graceful default). Add a loader lint that rejects an effort value outside EFFORTS — the DSCP 'unknown class → drop or default, never silently misroute' rule.

Direct anchor: grounding brief §1 'Every agent frontmatter across all 8 plugins hardcodes model: (opus/sonnet/haiku), zero effort: fields (0 of 24 in team-execution), no dispatch-time override lever anywhere except saga's readonly-verifier per-call pattern' — effort exists as a tier axis in execution_spec.py:53 but has no frontmatter representation to carry it.

title: Iterative-deepening escalate() primitive that walks a HALT up the tier ladder

Borrow iterative deepening from game-tree search: start at a shallow (cheap) tier and, on an inconclusive/HALT result, re-run one rung deeper until a budget stop — chess engines do exactly this with search depth. Add `tier_ladder.next_rung(tier)` returning the next stronger model / higher effort per the load-bearing ordering, and a bounded retry policy in the workflow harness so a cheap unit that HALTs escalates one rung and re-runs instead of failing the whole spec. This turns {#tier-vocab-ordering}'s 'tiers are ordered ladders' from a documented fact into executable behavior, and gives cost-optimal 'cheapest tier that succeeds' rather than pre-committing xhigh-Opus on everything.
basis: Source domain: iterative-deepening depth-first search (start shallow, deepen on inconclusive result until a resource bound). Builds on (does not cross) binding decision {#tier-vocab-ordering}: LEARNINGS.md:164 states tier tuples are ordered escalation ladders, and execution_spec.py:1474-1475 already does min(MODELS.index)/max(EFFORTS.index) upgrade-only merge — the ordering primitive exists for merging but is never exposed as a step-up-on-failure operation.

title: Model palette as a HAL driver-registry with explicit rank, not positional tuples

Adding Claude 6 (or a new fable-class model) becomes a single registry row with an explicit rank, not a fleet-wide edit where getting tuple position wrong silently mis-ranks the model below haiku (the exact #285 failure where appending 'fable' would have ranked it weaker than haiku with no validation error). Add a CI guard `check_tier_registry.py` asserting ranks are total-ordered and unique so a mis-ranked new entry fails loudly rather than mis-tiering merges.

Explicit rank rows separate the two contracts.

Define a three-layer cascade — plan default tier → team default → per-teammate override — where most-specific wins, and emit a resolved-tier audit line per teammate recording which layer set it ('teammate worker-saga: effort=high, source=per-teammate override; model=opus, source=team default'). This makes the override auditable and prevents the silent-mis-tier failure mode the fleet already fears, rather than a bare unlabeled effort knob.

title: Fleet-wide tier-vocab parity guard modeled on ISO 4217 currency-code validation
idea: Treat the tier palette as the theme's own metaphor makes literal — a currency — and enforce it the way payment systems enforce ISO 4217 currency codes: a central code registry plus validators everywhere that reject any code not in it. Add a repo-level test that statically scans every plugin's agent frontmatter, SKILL.md tier tables, and any config carrying model/effort strings, and asserts each string is a member of the canonical vocabulary module (from idea 1) — so the day fable/xhigh or a Claude 6 tier lands, any plugin still carrying a stale or misspelled tier fails CI instead of silently dispatching to a nonexistent model. title: Effort as a spendable budget under a Kubernetes-style ResourceQuota per run
idea: Give the effort dimension a cost weight and a run-level ceiling, borrowing Kubernetes ResourceQuota + QoS classes (Guaranteed/Burstable/BestEffort): pods declare resource requests, a namespace quota caps total spend, and the scheduler refuses admission past the cap. This turns effort from a per-unit label into a fleet-wide accounting unit — the operator sees 'this spec costs 4.2 budget units, ceiling 3.0' before it runs, matching the HALT-not-degrade posture from the /outcome campaign binding.
